comment:
<comment datatype="string"><i>E. coli</i> encodes two carbonic anhydrases, Can and CynT.  <i>cynT</i> is encoded in an operon with
<i>cynS</i>, the gene encoding cyanase, and its expression is inducible by cyanate [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7961413">Lamblin94</a>].  The biological
role of the CynT carbonic anhydrase is to prevent the depletion of endogenous bicarbonate due to rapid loss of CO<sub>2</sub>,
the product of the cyanase-catalyzed reaction, by diffusion out of the cell [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1740425">Guilloton92</a>].  CynT belongs to Clade A
of the &beta; class of carbonic anhydrases [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10978542">Smith00</a>].
<p>
The enzyme behaves as an oligomer of two or four subunits, depending on the presence of bicarbonate
[<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1740425">Guilloton92</a>].
<p>
At atmospheric concentrations of CO<sub>2</sub>, a <i>cynT</i> mutant is more sensitive to cyanate than a
<i>cynS</i> mutant and can not utilize cyanate as the sole source of nitrogen, although it produces active cyanase. 
However, at a high pCO<sub>2</sub> of 3%, it behaves like the wild type [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8444806">Guilloton93</a>].  After cyanate is depleted,
CynT is degraded rapidly at high pCO<sub>2</sub>, but only slowly at low pCO<sub>2</sub> [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8083164">Kozliak94</a>]. 
Growth inhibition by cyanate in the absence of carbonic anhydrase is not solely due to depletion of bicarbonate
[<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7768821">Kozliak95</a>].
<p>
Can has similarity to CynT, and induction of <i>cynT</i> expression suppresses phenotypes of a <i>can</i> mutant
[<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/14563877">Merlin03</a>].  A <i>can cynT</i> double mutant is only viable under high CO<sub>2</sub> conditions
[<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12784642">Hashimoto03</a>].
<p>
The product of the <i>cynT</i> gene was originally thought to be a cyanate permease [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/3049588">Sung88</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2670891">Sung89</a>]. 
<p>
Reviews: [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10978542">Smith00</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11268536">Kozliak00</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11696553">Tripp01</a>]</comment>

comment:
<comment datatype="string">In <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=ORGANISM&object=TAX-562"><i>Escherichia coli</i></a> <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-69">cyanate</a> can occur inside the cell as a result of nonenzymatic decomposition
of <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CARBAMOYL-P">carbamoyl phosphate</a>, and in the environment due to dissociation of <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=UREA">urea</a> and photooxidation of
<a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=HCN">hydrogen cyanide</a>.
Although cyanate at high concentrations is toxic to <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=ORGANISM&object=TAX-562"><i>Escherichia coli</i></a>, it can serve as a sole source of nitrogen due to
the production of <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=AMMONIA">ammonia</a> by <a href="/gene?orgid=META&id=CYANLY-MONOMER">cyanase</a> [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/3034861">Sung87</a>].  The cyanate degradation pathway therefore
serves the dual purpose of detoxification and nitrogen utilization [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7768821">Kozliak95</a>].  
<p>
Cyanase catalyzes the first step of the pathway, producing <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CARBON-DIOXIDE">CO<SUB>2</SUB></a> and the unstable compound
<a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CARBAMATE">carbamate</a>, which spontaneously decomposes to <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CARBON-DIOXIDE">CO<SUB>2</SUB></a> and <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=AMMONIA">ammonia</a>,
thus producing a source of nitrogen for growth.
The second enzyme of this pathway, carbonic anhydrase, is an essential component of the pathway.  In the
absence of carbonic anhydrase at atmospheric concentrations of <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CARBON-DIOXIDE">CO<SUB>2</SUB></a>, non-enzymatic hydration of
<a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CARBON-DIOXIDE">CO<SUB>2</SUB></a> is not sufficient to prevent depletion of the intracellular <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=HCO3">hydrogencarbonate</a> pool due to rapid
diffusion of <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CARBON-DIOXIDE">CO<SUB>2</SUB></a> [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8444806">Guilloton93</a>].
<p>
<a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=ORGANISM&object=TAX-294"><i>Pseudomonas fluorescens</i></a> NCIB 11764 is also capable of utilizing cyanate as a sole source of nitrogen for growth
[<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2495763">Kunz89</a>]. The induced enzymatic activity of extracts of cyanate grown <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=ORGANISM&object=TAX-294"><i>Pseudomonas fluorescens</i></a> NCIB
11764 cells was shown to be bicarbonate dependent and specific for cyanate, resembling
the enzymatic activity of cyanase as described in <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=ORGANISM&object=TAX-562"><i>Escherichia coli</i></a> [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2495763">Kunz89</a>].
</comment>

comment:
<comment datatype="string">Cyanase is an inducible enzyme in <i>E. coli</i> and was first reported and subsequently studied in
<i>E. coli</i> B [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/13775509">Taussig60</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/6994799">Anderson80</a>].  The cyanase operon may have evolved to function in
detoxification/decomposition of cyanate arising from intra- and extracellular activities [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2094285">Anderson90</a>].
<p>
It was shown that bicarbonate (HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>-</sup>) is a substrate of the enzyme, and that water does
not participate as a substrate [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/3110153">Johnson87</a>].  The initial product carbamate is unstable and spontaneously
decomposes to ammonia and carbon dioxide [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/6994799">Anderson80</a>].  The enzyme shows competitive substrate inhibition
by both substrates [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/3518792">Anderson86</a>].
<p>
The native enzyme from <i>E. coli</i> B has a molecular weight of ca. 150 kDa and thus appears to be a
homodecamer in solution [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/6994799">Anderson80</a>].  A crystal structure of cyanase was solved at 1.65 &Aring; resolution; it
showed a homodecamer composed of five dimers.  The structure allowed identification of the active site, which is
located between dimers and is comprised of residues from four adjacent subunits [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10801492">Walsh00</a>].
<p>
The free sulfhydryl group of the single cysteine residue is not required for catalytic activity, but plays a role in
stabilizing the decameric structure [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/3128546">Anderson88b</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8195141">Anderson94</a>].  The single histidine residue is also required for the
stability of the decamer and contributes to its catalytic properties [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8195141">Anderson94</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7947823">Anderson94a</a>].
<p>
A mutant lacking cyanase is more sensitive to cyanate than the wild type [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/3309165">Guilloton87</a>]; a
<i>cynS</i> mutant is not able to use cyanate as the sole source of nitrogen [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/3034861">Sung87</a>].
</comment>

comment:
<comment datatype="string"><i>E. coli</i> encodes two carbonic anhydrases, Can (carbonic anhydrase 2) and CynT (carbonic anhydrase 1).  Can belongs to Clade B of the &beta; class of carbonic anhydrases [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10978542">Smith00</a>].  Carbonic anhydrase 2 is essential for growth at amospheric pCO<sub>2</sub> [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12784642">Hashimoto03</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/14563877">Merlin03</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16738554">Baba06</a>].  Enzymatic activity of carbonic anhydrase 2 is pH-dependent [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11316870">Cronk01</a>].
<p>
Crystal structures of carbonic anhydrase 2 have been solved.  The crystal structure data as well as size exclusion chromatography indicate that the protein exists as a homotetramer in solution [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11316870">Cronk01</a>].  There is structural evidence for a noncatalytic binding site for bicarbonate [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16584170">Cronk06</a>].
<p>
A <i>can</i> mutant does not grow under normal atmospheric conditions, but the mutant can grow under conditions with a high exogenous or endogenous supply of CO<sub>2</sub>.  Expression of <i>cynT</i> suppresses phenotypes of a <i>can</i> mutant [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/14563877">Merlin03</a>].  A <i>can cynT</i> double mutant is only viable under high CO<sub>2</sub> conditions [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12784642">Hashimoto03</a>].
<p>
Expression of <i>can</i> is inversely proportional to the growth rate and does not depend on CO<sub>2</sub> levels [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/14563877">Merlin03</a>].  Under anaerobiosis, FNR represses <i>can</i> gene expression, but it is not known if this regulation is direct or indirect  [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12754220">Salmon03</a>].
<p>
Can: "<b>c</b>arbonic <b>an</b>hydrase" [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/14563877">Merlin03</a>]
<p>
Reviews: [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10978542">Smith00</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11268536">Kozliak00</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11696553">Tripp01</a>]
</comment>

<comment datatype="string">This enzyme, which is found in bacteria and plants, is used to decompose cyanate, which can be used as the sole source of nitrogen [[<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7768821">Kozliak95</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10801492">Walsh00</a>].
The reaction can be considered as the reverse of carbamate = cyanate + H2O', where this is assisted by reaction with bicarbonate and carbon dioxide [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/3110153">Johnson87</a>], and hence is classified in sub-subclass 4.2.1. Bicarbonate functions as a recycling substrate [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/3110153">Johnson87</a>].</comment>
